standard.title: Data represented as numbers
standard.description: Explain how digital systems represent all data using numbers
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can recognise different types of data and explore how the same data can be represented differently depending on context (AC9TDI4K03). They understand that data exists in different forms (text, images, numbers). They have not yet connected the idea that digital systems ultimately represent all these different data types as numbers.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how digital systems represent all types of data — text, images, sound — as numbers, and understand that the data type determines what operations can be performed.

nodes.label: Text as numbers
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how text characters are represented as numbers in a digital system
nodes.minimum_width: Convert letters in a short message to numbers using a positional scheme (e.g. A=1, B=2) and explain that digital systems use similar numeric encoding for text
nodes.typical_width: Explain that each character in a digital system is assigned a number (like ASCII or Unicode); demonstrate with examples how text characters — letters, numbers, symbols — each map to a unique number that the system stores and processes
wider: Investigate how Unicode allows characters from non-English scripts (e.g. Chinese, Arabic, First Nations language characters) to be encoded numerically — why a single scheme matters for global communication
Explore how emoji are also assigned numeric codes — explaining that an emoji is stored as a number just like the letter 'A' is

response_modes.reason: Students readily accept that the number '5' is stored as a number, but resist the idea that the letter 'A' is also stored as a number — it seems like a category error. Multiple encoding contexts (letters, emoji, non-Latin scripts) help students generalise: all characters, regardless of type, are ultimately numbers.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Unicode/non-Latin script direction is genuinely rich — it connects numeric representation to questions of language equity and the design decisions behind universal standards. First Nations language context is directly applicable here.
success_criteria: Explains that text characters are stored as numbers in a digital system
Can demonstrate a simple letter-to-number conversion
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have not grasped that data is represented as numbers cannot engage with N2's data type reasoning — if a student does not accept that 'A' and 65 are the same stored value in different interpretations, the concept that type determines operations has no foundation.

nodes.label: Data type determines what you can do
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how the data type used to represent data changes what operations can be performed on it
nodes.minimum_width: Give one example showing that the same value behaves differently depending on its data type — e.g. adding '3' + '4' gives 7 when they are numbers but '34' when they are strings
nodes.typical_width: Explain that numbers support arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction) while text supports string operations (joining, searching); demonstrate both with examples; explain why digital systems need to know which type they are working with
wider: Investigate how treating a phone number as a number versus a string causes real problems — adding phone numbers is meaningless, but searching within them (e.g. all numbers starting with 04) requires string operations
Explore how images are also represented as numbers (each pixel has a numeric colour value) and what kinds of operations this enables — adjusting brightness by changing pixel values mathematically

response_modes.reason: Students often treat data types as arbitrary naming conventions rather than a meaningful distinction. Concrete cases where the type matters (phone number as number vs string, pixel values as arithmetic) help students see that the type determines what operations make sense — not just what the value looks like.

The reasoning pattern here (identify data → identify operation → check if type supports operation → predict outcome) is the key skill. Scaffolding this as an explicit reasoning chain prevents students from guessing rather than reasoning.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The image-as-numbers direction is rich — it extends the numeric representation idea to a visually intuitive domain and opens up the idea that images can be processed mathematically, which is foundational for later AI/computer vision concepts.
success_criteria: Gives a correct example where the same value behaves differently based on data type
Explains in plain language why data type affects what operations are possible
